title: Evaluation of acoustical conditions for speech communication in working elementary school classrooms
authors: Sato, H. and Bradley, J. S., 2008
research_question: To obtain more representative and accurate indications of the acoustical quality of conditions for speech communication during actual teaching activities in elementary school classrooms, and to better understand how to improve speech communication between teachers and students.

participants.description: 27 traditional rectangular elementary school classrooms (out of 41 initially investigated, including 16 grade 1, 12 grade 3, and 13 grade 6 classrooms) near Ottawa, Canada. The mean number of children present during measurements was 20.6 (S.D. = 4.5).
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but implies selection of active elementary school classrooms in the Ottawa area.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 41 active elementary school classrooms, with detailed acoustical measurements made in 27 traditional rectangular classrooms. Measurements were taken in both occupied (with students and teacher during teaching activities) and unoccupied conditions (without students, but with ambient noise sources).

measures.instrument: Impulse response measurements using sine sweep signal, processed by RAMSoft-3 software, calculated by backward integration of octave band filtered impulse responses (-5 to -35 dB range)
Impulse response measurements using sine sweep signal, processed by RAMSoft-3 software

measures.instrument: Logarithmic ratio of sound energy from measured impulse response to free field response at 10m, calibrated using directivity pattern of sound source

findings.quote: When the classrooms were occupied, reverberation times were decreased by approximately 10%.

findings.mechanism: Decrease in late-arriving energy (1.84 dBA) and early-reflection energy (0.49 dBA) due to student absorption.
findings.quote: C50 values increased on average by 1.34 dBA when the rooms were occupied compared to the unoccupied conditions.

findings.mechanism: Added absorption by students.

findings.mechanism: Longer reverberation times mean more sustained reflections.
findings.quote: Glate values vary little with distance and vary more with reverberation time.

findings.mechanism: As T60 increases, late-arriving sound energy increases more steeply than early sound, reducing the ratio.
findings.quote: C50 values decrease with increasing reverberation time.

findings.mechanism: Existing noise sources (e.g., HVAC, external noise) in classrooms.
findings.quote: The average noise levels in the unoccupied classrooms were more than the 35dBA recommended by ANSI S12.60 [11].

findings.mechanism: Teacher's vocal effort during teaching.
findings.quote: For this data the mean speech level was 60.4 dBA (S.D. = 4.4 dBA)

findings.mechanism: Combination of background noise and student activity noise.
findings.quote: and the mean ambient noise level 49.1 dBA (S.D.= 4.3 dBA).

findings.mechanism: High noise levels relative to speech levels.
findings.quote: only 6.25% of the active class situations satisfy the S/N ≥ 15dBA requirement for 12-13 year old children to get near perfect word recognition scores [3].

findings.mechanism: Lombard effect: teachers increase vocal effort in noisy environments.
findings.quote: Fig. 13 shows the relation between room-average speech and noise levels. They are well correlated (correlation coefficient, r = 0.82, p < 0.001).

findings.mechanism: Lombard effect.
findings.quote: Fig. 13 shows a 0.75dB increase of speech level per 1dB increase of noise level.

findings.mechanism: Noise generated by children's activity.
findings.quote: On average, in the active classrooms, the noise generated by children increases the noise level by 5 dBA and the increases vary up to a maximum of 10 dBA relative to the occupied levels in the same classrooms without student activity.

findings.mechanism: Lombard effect: children talk louder to be heard over ambient noise.
findings.quote: There is an obvious trend in Fig. 14 for the student activity noise levels to increase with increasing ambient noise levels in the rooms without any student activity. This is another example of the Lombard effect.

findings.mechanism: Direct relationship between mid-frequency and A-weighted C50.
findings.quote: The relation between C50(mid) and C50(A) is C50(A) = 0.98*C50(mid) + 1.9, r = 0.92, p < 0.001.

findings.mechanism: Weak correlation, noise levels are primarily from direct sound and early reflections.
findings.quote: and reverberation times (r = 0.33, p <0.01).

findings.mechanism: Noise levels are mostly due to direct sound and early reflections from noise sources, not significantly affected by absorption in this range.
findings.quote: values between 0.3 and 0.6 s have no significant effect on noise levels. That is, adding absorption would not be expected to reduce these noise levels.

findings.antecedent: Reverberation time (T60) of 0.3s (for average classroom conditions at 6m distance)
findings.mechanism: Optimal balance between useful early reflections and detrimental late reflections and noise.
findings.quote: Fig. 17 suggests an optimum reverberation time of about 0.3s.

findings.antecedent: Reverberation time (T60) between 0.2s and 0.5s (for average classroom conditions at 6m distance)
findings.mechanism: Slight deviation from optimal T60 leads to minor reduction in U50(A).
findings.quote: reducing the reverberation time to 0.2 s or increasing it to about 0.5 s only reduces U50(A) values by slightly over 1 dBA and hence near ideal conditions can be achieved over quite a broad range of reverberation time values.

findings.mechanism: Less need for early-reflection energy to achieve adequate speech-to-noise ratios.
findings.quote: Lower background noise levels allow shorter reverberation times because adequate speech-to-noise ratios can be achieved with the help of less early-reflection energy.

findings.mechanism: Longer reverberation time is needed to increase the early sound component and compensate for lower speech level.
findings.quote: A lower speech level would shift the optimum U50(A) value to a longer reverberation time to increase the early sound component.

mechanisms: Lombard effect: Teachers and students increase their voice levels in response to higher background noise levels to maintain audibility.
Sound absorption by occupants: Students act as sound absorbers, reducing reverberation time and altering early-to-late energy ratios.
Early reflections: Early-arriving sound reflections enhance speech levels and intelligibility, especially at greater distances from the speaker.
Late reflections: Late-arriving sound reflections can mask direct and early speech sounds, degrading intelligibility.

Prediction of sound fields: Modified Barron's revised theory can accurately predict sound strength components in classrooms, indicating the relative contributions of direct, early, and late sound energy.
implementation_implications: Excessive noise levels are a significant problem in elementary school classrooms, often exceeding recommended standards, making ideal speech communication difficult.
Reducing unoccupied noise levels is crucial, as it can also reduce student activity noise due to the Lombard effect.
Adding sound absorption material is unlikely to be effective for reducing student activity noise, which is primarily direct and early-reflected sound from nearby students.
Very short reverberation times should be avoided, as they reduce beneficial early reflections that enhance teacher voice levels and reduce vocal strain.

Classroom design should focus on reducing late-arriving sound levels at distant listening positions to ensure useful direct and early reflections are well above detrimental sounds, rather than solely targeting an optimum reverberation time.
Teachers should be aware of the importance of controlling student activity noise during oral communication.

limitations: The sound power level of the sound source for measurements was not successfully measured at the time of classroom measurements, requiring a calibration procedure based on estimated angles and free field calculations.
The exact angles from the sound source to each receiver in the classrooms were not known, requiring the use of approximate average angles for calibration.
The distribution technique for separating speech and noise levels could not be applied to open-plan classrooms due to poor isolation and similar voice levels from adjacent teachers.
The current analyses only include A-weighted SNR values, and further work is required to obtain octave band signal-to-noise ratios and other measures like Speech Transmission Index.
The simple U50(A) measure assumes a particular combination of room acoustics and SNR values is best correlated with speech intelligibility scores, but other combinations might be more successful.
The time window used to define 'early-arriving' sound needs further investigation.
The study's findings on relationships between room acoustics factors, speech, and noise levels are largely due to the limited range of acoustical conditions found in the measured classrooms.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Detailed acoustical measurements were made in 41 working elementary school classrooms near Ottawa, Canada to obtain more representative and more accurate indications of the acoustical quality of conditions for speech communication during actual teaching activities. This paper describes the room acoustics characteristics and noise environment of 27 traditional rectangular classrooms from the 41 measured rooms. The purpose of the work was to better understand how to improve speech communication between teachers and students. The study found, that on average, the students experienced: teacher speech levels of 60.4dBA, noise levels of 49.1dBA, and a mean speech-to-noise ratio of 11dBA during teaching activities. The mean reverberation time in the occupied classrooms was 0.41s, which was 10% less than in the unoccupied rooms. The reverberation time measurements were used to determine the average absorption added by each student. Detailed analyses of early and late-arriving speech sounds showed these sound levels could be predicted quite accurately and suggest improved approaches to room acoustics design.
